topic.en: What the text is about: how the railways forced towns to give up local noon and how time zones grew out of it.
topic.kk: Мәтін не туралы: темір жол қалаларды жергілікті түстен қалай бас тартқызды және содан уақыт белдеулері қалай шықты.
topic.ru: О чём текст: как железные дороги заставили города отказаться от местного полдня и как из этого выросли часовые пояса.

paragraphs.text: Until the middle of the nineteenth century, noon was a local fact. Each town set its clocks by the sun, so that midday came when the sun stood highest over that particular place, and a traveller moving west gained a few minutes with every hundred kilometres. Nobody minded, because nobody could move fast enough for the difference to matter. A coach took two days to cover a distance that changed local time by ten minutes, and ten minutes was less than the accuracy of the journey itself.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The railway made the difference intolerable. A timetable has to state a single time for a departure, and a line running east to west passed through dozens of towns whose clocks disagreed. The first solution was to print conversion tables in the timetable, which worked for clerks and not for passengers. Railway companies then began running on one time, usually that of their head office, so that a station clock might show the company hour on one face and the town hour on the other.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Accidents sharpened the argument. Where two trains shared a single track and their positions were controlled by telegraph, a minute of disagreement between the two ends of a line was a collision waiting to happen. The safety case was what carried the argument in most countries; the convenience of passengers was a secondary consideration and is the one the histories tend to remember. By the 1850s the main British lines had standardised, and legal time followed the railways rather than leading them.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Resistance was local and stubborn. Town councils objected to having their noon set by a company in another city, and for years some municipal clocks carried two minute hands. The objection was not merely sentimental: a town whose legal business, licensing hours and court sittings ran on local time could find itself in a dispute with a railway operating on another. Several court cases turned on which noon had been meant, and one famous case was decided against a man who had arrived by the clock in the square.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The global system was agreed in 1884, at a conference in Washington attended by delegates from twenty-five countries. It chose the meridian of Greenwich as the starting point, largely because most of the world’s shipping already used charts based on it, and it proposed a day of twenty-four hours counted from midnight. The conference had no power to compel anyone, and adoption took decades: France kept Paris time for its domestic purposes until 1911, defining it in law as Greenwich time delayed by nine minutes and twenty-one seconds rather than naming Greenwich at all.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Zones were never purely geographical, and they are not now. A zone is drawn where a government decides, and the decisions follow economics and politics: a country may take one zone for the whole of its territory so that the capital and the provinces keep the same office hours, or shift its clocks to sit with a trading partner. The result is a map with boundaries that swing far from the meridians, and several places where crossing a border changes the time by three quarters of an hour rather than a whole one.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The clock has since become an instrument rather than a description. Summer time, introduced widely during the First World War to save fuel, moves the working day relative to daylight without moving the sun; the argument about whether it still saves anything has run for a century and is unresolved in the evidence, though the effects on sleep in the days after a change are measurable and consistent. Whatever is decided, the decision will be about what the hour is for, not about what time it is.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: What the history shows is how quickly an arrangement becomes invisible. The idea that the whole of a large country should share a single noon was, within living memory of the people who introduced it, an obvious imposition by a private company on a town that had kept its own time for centuries. It is now so ordinary that the older arrangement sounds like a curiosity, which is a reasonable description of most of the infrastructure we argue about today. The next such arrangement is probably being imposed somewhere now, by a company, for a practical reason, over the objections of people who will not be asked again once their grandchildren have grown up with it.
paragraphs.label: H
